criteria.name: Mission concept and rationale — What will it do, who are the users, why is it needed?
criteria.reasoning: The rationale and users are well articulated, but quantitative mission requirements (revisit times, spectral bands, payload mass/power) are lacking.

evidence.quote: A near-real-time relay to monitoring stations on the ground would allow marine and conservation scientists to more accurately predict and react
This tool could be applied to a new satellite over the Great Barrier Reef.

criteria.name: Project plan — How you plan to complete the assignment, including either a Gantt chart or a timetable and information sources you plan to use
criteria.reasoning: A Gantt chart and task breakdown are provided, but planned information sources are only loosely mentioned without specific literature/databases, and contingencies are absent.

evidence.quote: The earlier weeks will consist of researching existing satellites – including their creation, deployment, orbit, structure, and use.

criteria.name: Preliminary progress — Technical content and evidence of sufficient work done to date
criteria.reasoning: No actual technical data, calculations, or simulation results for the proposed mission are presented; only completion of generic software tutorials is claimed.

criteria.name: Report presentation
criteria.reasoning: The layout is readable and neat, but references are raw URLs and Image 1 lacks a formal figure number and caption.

technical_issues.issue: Proposed a 'geostationary orbit at an altitude of 600 km'. Geostationary orbit physically requires an altitude of ~35,786 km above the equator.

overall: Good concept rationale and clear structure, but technical progress is missing actual engineering work, and proposed orbital mechanics contains a major conceptual error (GEO at 600 km).

feedback.summary: You established a strong rationale and identified relevant users for your Great Barrier Reef monitoring concept, presenting your work with clear structure. To improve, address critical technical details in your orbital mechanics, develop quantified mission requirements, and include concrete technical calculations rather than generic software tutorials. Additionally, strengthen your project plan with contingencies and professional formatting.
next_steps: Correct the orbital parameters in your preliminary design: a true geostationary orbit requires ~35,786 km, whereas 600 km represents low Earth orbit (LEO).
Produce concrete technical results in your next report, such as payload sizing, power budgets, or initial STK orbital simulations tailored to the mission.
Format all citations with complete bibliographic details rather than raw URLs, and add formal figure numbers and descriptive captions to visuals like Image 1.

criteria.C1: You clearly articulated the mission rationale and identified user needs for monitoring the reef. To reach Accomplished, define quantitative requirements—such as revisit rates, spectral bands, and payload mass and power constraints—and integrate supporting literature.
criteria.C2: Your task breakdown and Gantt chart in Image 1 map out the schedule well. To achieve an Accomplished level, integrate specific literature and database sources, and incorporate clear contingency planning and risk management for potential project variations.
criteria.C3: Completing STK tutorials shows familiarisation, but no mission-specific engineering calculations or simulation outputs were provided. To reach Accomplished, include initial preliminary results—such as coverage analysis, delta-v budgets, or mass estimations—with clear engineering interpretations.
criteria.C4: Your document structure is neat and readable. To reach Accomplished, ensure all visual elements like Image 1 feature formal numbering and captions, and replace raw URLs in your reference list with fully structured academic citations.
